catalog_quote: In addition to the above vowels there is a shwa, a short central spread vowel, on which there is no tonal contrast. ... In these latter cases (and perhaps in some of the former ...) a syllable containing such a vowel is a reduced syllable. ... The Burmese and Arakanese word can be defined by juncture phenomena as described in Sprigg 1957. Burmese and Arakanese both have numerous words with reduced syllable, one reduced syllable in a two-syllable word; and the first or second, or even the first two in a three-syllable word. Few syllables with etymological/orthographic stop-finals have reduced forms. In many cases the full-syllable form may occur in slower, more formal speech. [p.198, sec. 5 Tones] The Arakanese tones have similar realizations to those in Burmese: heavy: /ˋ/ high intensity; falling contour, generally fairly high Fo, breathy phonation; level: Ø low intensity; level contour, generally fairly low Fo, normal phonation; creaky: /ˊ/ creaky voicing, slightly falling contour, high Fo (stop-final): /ʔ/ short duration; very high Fo, final stop and no juncture voicing following. Some words have creaky tone in Burmese, but heavy tone in Arakanese, or less frequently vice versa. [Okell 1995 p.7, sec. 2.2.1.1 TONES] heavy ... creaky ... low ... stop ... weak [p.16] Weakening in AR occurs in the same way, and with the same voicing pattern, as in SB. ... AR however makes more extensive use of weakening than SB.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Arakanese/Rakhine is a Burmese-type tone language (heavy, level/low, creaky, stop/checked tones on every full syllable; Okell adds a fifth 'weak' category). Toneless schwa ('reduced'/'weak') syllables occur only in non-final position (first syllable of disyllables; first and/or second of trisyllables), so the word-final syllable is always a full tone-bearing syllable. None of the descriptions states a word-stress rule or uses 'stress' for word prominence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Bradley p.189: full-syllable forms may replace reduced ones in slow, formal speech; Arakanese reduces nasal-final syllables less than Burmese, but reduces some items Burmese does not. Okell p.17: some words weak in Standard Burmese are full syllables in Arakanese (e.g. /tEn-/ words). Huziwara p.254: Marma neutral tone on Cə syllables is non-distinctive; pitch of Cə varies with the following tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonotactics of reduced vs full syllables ('the Burmese and Arakanese word can be defined by juncture phenomena'); tones are syllable/lexical. No phrase-level stress discussed (Okell notes only sentence-final intonation effects for Intha/Tavoyan, not Arakanese).
new_statements.identity_note: Okell 1995 and Bradley 1985 describe Arakanese of Sittwe (Akyab) District / Mrauk-U, i.e. Rakhine proper = rakh1245 [rki]. Huziwara 2003 describes Marma of Rajasthali, Chittagong Hill Tracts, Bangladesh (ISO 639-3 rmz; Glottolog treats Marma as a separate languoid under the Arakanese group - code not verified here); Okell (p.3) reports Marma as phonologically near-identical to Sittwe Arakanese apart from /ky khy gy/ for Sittwe /c ch j/. All three agree on the prosodic type (four tones + toneless reduced presyllables).

tone_statements.quote: There are 3 types of syllables: pre-syllable, minor syllable and major syllable. The structure of the syllable is C1 (C3) (C4) V1 (C2). ... There are 21 vowel phonemes which are divided into 3 sets: 1) six plain vowels: /i, e, a, u, o, ɔ/. 2) Eight glottal vowels: /iˀ, ɛˀ, aˀ, ɔˀ, eiˀ, ouˀ, aiˀ, auˀ/. And 3) seven nasal vowels: /ɛ̃, ã, ɔ̃, eĩ, oũ, aĩ, aũ/. There are four tones: (1) high-rising-falling, (2) high-falling and (3) high-rising ending with a glottal constriction of the breath (slow glottal closure).

tone_statements.quote: There are three contrastive tones in Arakanese Burmese : /1,2,3/ These three tonemes function in major and minor syllable. The plain and the nasal vowels can bear all three of tones while the glottal vowels can bear only one tone : high falling. Beside these three, there is another one, the short mid tone.It only occurs in a zero-stressed syllable in which the vowel is very short and always has mid central pitch. ... No tone-contrast is found on such syllables. ... [Table 10] /1/ low low-rising-falling ... /2/ high high-falling ... /3/ creaky high-rising
